newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Easier investment rules fuel Zimbabwe share gains.
newsitem.headline: Easier investment rules fuel Zimbabwe share gains.

text.p: Zimbabwean stocks continued their upward march on Thursday with brokers saying an increase in the level of permitted foreign shareholdings had further spurred the local bourse's bull-run.
The key 57-share industrial index jumped 76.04 points -- or 1.2 percent -- to a record 6,241.30.
"The market is looking very upbeat. There's a lot of good news around, including yesterday's announcement on foreign investment, so that's added to the bull-run," one broker said.
The central Reserve Bank on Wednesday raised to 40 percent from 35 percent the maximum holding permitted to foreign shareholders in a Zimbabwean company.
Reserve Bank governor Leonard Tsumba also said a single investor could now own up to 10 percent of the equity of a listed company, compared to five percent previously.

Exchange deputy chairman Trudy Cashel and some brokers said the measures could see a return of foreign buying in a couple of companies which had reached the 35 percent limit. These included conglomerate TA Holdings which traded 17 cents higher at 147 on Thursday and Wankie Colliery Co Ltd which rose 10 cents to 340.
"TA (Holdings) had a problem because a few foreign trades were stopped because they had gotten to the 35 percent limit so this announcement came at the right time," one broker said.

Zimbabwe first opened its stock exchange to foreigners in May 1993 under Western-backed economic reforms started in 1991. Since then, the exchange has attracted net foreign investment inflows amounting to U.S.$140 million.

Brokers said foreigners were interested in a wide range of counters, from blue-chips such as conglomerate Delta, consumer- related and tourism stocks like TA Holdings and Zimsun Ltd, to banks and gold and nickel miners.

Cashel and the brokers said they expected Wednesday's measures to propel the local bourse higher, anchoring its place as one of the world's top emerging market performers, a tag it has boasted for the past three years.

The market has been on a bull-run since mid-August, spurred by prospects of lower interest rates after the Reserve Bank cut its key rediscount rate to 27.5 percent from 29.5 percent after annual inflation fell to 22 percent in July from 28 percent in January. A string of good corporate results also added to the upward trend.

Brokers and Savvas Kyriakides, managing director of stock market and economic analysts Dataworld, said the exchange managed to shrug off the financial impact of a two-week strike by civil servants which paralysed key essential services because the good news outweighed the bad.

"The stock market has been so used to bad news for a long time -- high inflation, high interest rates, drought -- that now there is a lot of good news, it is concentrating on that instead of the bad," Kyriakides told Reuters.
